plan: Ten new SAT R&W items weighted toward upper difficulty (6 hard): qualified (WIC, near-synonym trap "ambiguous"), glassfrog clotting inference, noise-tolerance evidence (support for an "X alone cannot predict" claim), Antikythera cross-text with a partial concession, two-part quantitative claim requiring totals and percent changes, function of a closing quotation, simple past with a dated event, semicolon boundary with a quoted label, illustration transition, rhetorical synthesis for significance. Topics checked against the live bank before drafting. Relabelled to the lower of the two blind ratings: authored 6 hard / 2 medium, both blind solvers rated none hard, so final labels are 5 medium / 5 easy (difficulty provisional). After the blind solves, only the S042-10 setup line was reworded ("While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:") at the second solver's suggestion; stem, choices and key unchanged. Both solvers flagged the key as the longest choice in 02, 05 and 10 (minor).

passages.title: A cautious endorsement
passages.text: The panel's report on the new water filter was carefully ______: it confirmed that the device removed lead in laboratory tests but declined to say whether it would perform as well in older homes, where pipes shed metal particles unevenly.

passages.title: Glassfrogs at rest
passages.text: Glassfrogs have transparent skin and muscle, yet their red blood would ordinarily make them easy for predators to spot. Researchers found that when a glassfrog sleeps, it removes nearly 90 percent of its red blood cells from circulation and packs them into its liver, whose reflective surface hides them; when the frog wakes and becomes active, the cells return to its bloodstream. Remarkably, the packed cells do not form the clots that such dense crowding of blood cells causes in most animals. This finding has drawn interest from medical researchers, since it suggests that ______

passages.title: Noise and nests
passages.text: Ecologist Clinton Francis compared nesting birds near natural-gas wells fitted with noisy compressors and near quiet wells in New Mexico. Western scrub jays, which eat other birds' eggs, avoided the noisy sites. As a result, some species, such as black-chinned hummingbirds, nested more successfully near the noisy compressors than near quiet wells. Francis argues that the effects of noise on a bird species cannot be predicted from how well that species tolerates noise alone.

passages.title: Two views of the Antikythera mechanism
passages.text:
Text 1
The Antikythera mechanism, a bronze gearwork recovered from a shipwreck dated to the first century BCE, predicted eclipses and tracked the positions of the Sun and Moon. Some historians argue that its precision implies a long tradition of similar devices, now lost, since a machine this refined is unlikely to have been the first of its kind.

Text 2
Other historians note that the mechanism's gear teeth were cut by hand and are slightly irregular, and that some of its predictions would have drifted noticeably within a few years. To these historians, the imperfections suggest a workshop still solving basic problems of construction rather than one refining a mature craft. Yet they grant that metal objects were routinely melted down for reuse, so the absence of other such devices proves little.

passages.title: Shared bikes
passages.text:
A city analyst compared daily trips on its shared-bike system before and after it added 40 docking stations in outlying neighborhoods.
Average weekday trips: central stations 5,200 before and 5,150 after; outlying stations 300 before and 1,450 after.
Average weekend trips: central stations 3,100 before and 3,050 after; outlying stations 250 before and 1,900 after.
The analyst concluded that the new stations increased total ridership rather than merely shifting riders away from central stations, and that the increase was proportionally larger on weekends.

passages.title: A novelist's revision
passages.text: When the novelist Kaya Ostrander revised her first book for a new edition twenty years after it appeared, readers expected her to modernize its dated slang. Instead, she left every line of dialogue untouched and rewrote only the narrator's commentary, removing the knowing asides that had once explained the characters to the reader. The characters' speech, she wrote in a preface, was "a record of how people sounded"; the narrator's explanations were "a record only of how much I distrusted my readers."

passages.title: Seed banks
passages.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores duplicate samples of seeds held by gene banks around the world. In 2015, researchers at a gene bank in Syria, whose collection had been damaged by war, ______ the first withdrawal from the vault, using the duplicates to rebuild their collection in Lebanon and Morocco.

passages.title: An old map
passages.text: In 1507, the cartographer Martin Waldseemüller printed a world map that was the first to label the newly encountered lands across the Atlantic ______ only a single copy of the roughly 1,000 printed copies survives.

passages.title: Measuring a coastline
passages.text: In the mid-twentieth century, the scientist Lewis Fry Richardson noticed that the measured length of a coastline grows as the measuring stick gets shorter, because a shorter stick follows smaller inlets and bends. ______ the coastline of Britain measured with a 200-kilometer stick is about 2,400 kilometers long, but measured with a 50-kilometer stick it is about 3,400 kilometers.

passages.title: Notes on a dye
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In 1856, 18-year-old William Perkin tried to make quinine, a malaria drug, from coal tar.
- The attempt failed, but it produced a purple substance.
- Perkin found the substance could dye silk and did not fade in sunlight or washing.
- He named it mauveine and opened a factory to produce it.
- Before mauveine, purple dyes came from sources such as sea snails and were very expensive.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: declined to say whether it would perform as well in older homes
candidates.explanation: The report gave approval but limited it: it confirmed laboratory results while withholding judgment about older homes. Approval with stated limits is "qualified."

B.rationale: The report confirmed the device worked in laboratory tests, so it did not reject the filter.

C.rationale: Declining to make a claim about older homes is the opposite of unrestrained praise.

D.rationale: The report was clear about what it confirmed and what it would not claim; it limited its claims rather than leaving them unclear.

hints: Does the report give unlimited approval, no approval, or approval with limits?
candidates.remember: "Qualified" praise is approval with reservations; it does not mean unclear.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: glassfrogs are more transparent while they are active than while they are asleep.
choices.B: most animals could avoid predators by storing their blood cells in the liver.
choices.C: the glassfrog's liver produces most of the red blood cells that circulate when the frog is active.
choices.D: glassfrogs may have a mechanism for preventing clots that could inform efforts to reduce clotting in humans.

candidates.evidence: the packed cells do not form the clots
candidates.explanation: The surprising detail is that densely packed blood cells do not clot in glassfrogs, although they would in most animals. That is why medical researchers are interested: the frogs may reveal a way to prevent clotting.

A.rationale: The text says the frogs hide their red cells during sleep, so they would be more transparent asleep, not awake.

B.rationale: The text says crowding causes clots in most animals, so it does not suggest the strategy would work for them.

C.rationale: The liver stores and hides the cells; the text never says it produces them.

hints: Why would medical researchers, not just biologists, care?

strategy.explanation: Find the surprising fact the last sentence is responding to.

candidates.remember: The completion must connect to the detail that explains the stated reaction.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (supporting a claim)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Francis's argument?

choices.A: Black-chinned hummingbirds sang at higher pitches near noisy compressors than near quiet wells.
choices.B: A bird species that tolerates noise well nested less successfully near noisy wells because a predator that ignores noise moved into those areas.
choices.C: Western scrub jays avoided noisy areas in several other states as well as in New Mexico.
choices.D: Bird species that avoid noise had fewer nests near noisy wells than near quiet wells.

candidates.evidence: cannot be predicted from how well that species tolerates noise alone
candidates.explanation: Francis claims tolerance alone does not predict outcomes because other species, such as predators, respond to noise too. A noise-tolerant species doing worse because of a predator's response would show exactly that.

A.rationale: A change in song does not show that noise effects depend on factors other than the species' own tolerance.

C.rationale: This extends one finding about jays but says nothing about whether tolerance alone predicts a species' success.

D.rationale: This is what tolerance alone would predict, so it does not support the claim that tolerance is insufficient.

hints: What else, besides a species' own tolerance, affects the outcome in the text?

strategy.explanation: Restate the claim, then find the choice that shows a second factor at work.

candidates.remember: Support for "X alone cannot predict Y" shows a case where another factor changes Y.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the historians in Text 2 most likely respond to the argument in Text 1?

choices.A: They would accept that the device belongs to a long tradition but argue that the tradition began only shortly before the shipwreck.
choices.B: They would agree that the device was refined but argue that refinement alone cannot show that other devices existed.
choices.C: They would question the premise that the device is highly refined, while agreeing that the lack of surviving devices does not settle the matter.
choices.D: They would reject the argument because no other devices like it have ever been found.

candidates.evidence: so the absence of other such devices proves little
candidates.explanation: Text 1's argument rests on the device's precision. Text 2 challenges that premise with evidence of imperfection, but concedes that missing devices are weak evidence either way, since metal was melted down.

A.rationale: Text 2 reads the imperfections as signs of an immature craft, so it does not accept the long-tradition conclusion.

B.rationale: Text 2 disputes the refinement itself, pointing to irregular teeth and drifting predictions.

D.rationale: Text 2 explicitly says the absence of other devices proves little, so they would not rely on it.

hints: Which part of the Text 1 argument does Text 2 challenge, and which does it concede?

strategy.explanation: Separate the premise (precision) from the evidence about missing devices.

candidates.remember: Cross-text responses can disagree with one point and concede another.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes data that support both parts of the analyst's conclusion?

choices.A: Central trips fell by only 50 on each day type while outlying trips rose by far more, and total weekend trips grew by about 48 percent compared with about 20 percent on weekdays.
choices.B: Outlying weekend trips (1,900) exceeded outlying weekday trips (1,450) after the stations were added.
choices.C: Weekday trips at outlying stations rose by 1,150, while weekend trips at outlying stations rose by 1,650.
choices.D: Central stations still had more weekday trips than outlying stations after the new stations were added.

candidates.evidence: increased total ridership rather than merely shifting riders away from central stations
candidates.explanation: Totals went from 5,500 to 6,600 on weekdays (+20%) and from 3,350 to 4,950 on weekends (+47.8%). Central trips barely changed, so riders were not just shifted. Only choice A addresses both parts.

B.rationale: This compares two "after" values but shows neither a gain in total ridership nor a proportional comparison of increases.

C.rationale: This supports a larger weekend increase in raw numbers but ignores the central-station data needed to rule out a mere shift of riders.

D.rationale: This is true but supports neither part of the conclusion.

hints: How many parts does the conclusion have? Check each choice against both.

strategy.explanation: Compute total trips before and after for each day type.

candidates.remember: A two-part claim needs data for both parts.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the quotation from the preface in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It shows that Ostrander regretted the slang in her characters' dialogue.
choices.B: It explains the reasoning behind the unexpected choice the text describes.
choices.C: It reveals that readers had criticized the narrator's commentary in the first edition.
choices.D: It introduces a new topic, Ostrander's attitude toward her readers, that the text goes on to develop.

candidates.evidence: Instead, she left every line of dialogue untouched
candidates.explanation: The text sets up an expectation (modernized slang) and a surprising choice (dialogue untouched, commentary rewritten). The quotation gives Ostrander's reasons for that choice.

A.rationale: She kept the dialogue as a record of how people sounded, so she did not regret it.

C.rationale: The preface describes Ostrander's own view of the commentary; no reader criticism is mentioned.

D.rationale: The quotation ends the text and explains the revision already described; nothing further is developed.

hints: What surprise does the text describe, and what does the quotation add?

strategy.explanation: Label each part: expectation, surprising choice, explanation.

candidates.remember: A closing quotation often supplies the reason for a choice the text has described.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The sentence describes a completed action at a specific past time, so the simple past "made" is correct.

A.rationale: The present perfect does not fit an action tied to a specific past year, 2015.

B.rationale: A participle cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence's subject "researchers."

D.rationale: The past perfect progressive implies an ongoing action before another past event; the withdrawal was a single completed event.

hints: Find the time marker in the sentence.
candidates.remember: A specific past time calls for the simple past.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: Two independent clauses ("...label the lands 'America'" and "today only a single copy...survives") need a semicolon, and the introductory "today" takes a comma.

A.rationale: A comma alone cannot join the two independent clauses, creating a comma splice.

B.rationale: Without punctuation after "America," the clauses run together and "today" seems to modify the label.

C.rationale: The comma creates a comma splice, and no comma follows "today" to set off the introductory word.

hints: How many independent clauses are there?

strategy.explanation: Find where the first clause ends.

candidates.remember: Join two independent clauses with a semicolon, not a comma.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.explanation: The second sentence gives a specific case of the pattern Richardson noticed, so "For example" fits.

B.rationale: The data agree with Richardson's observation rather than contrasting with it.

C.rationale: The figures illustrate the observation; they are not a result of Richardson's noticing it.

D.rationale: Nothing in the first sentence would make the figures surprising.

hints: Does the second sentence contrast with, result from, or illustrate the first?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: A specific instance of a general claim calls for an illustration transition.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain why mauveine's discovery mattered. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 1856, William Perkin, who was 18 years old, tried to make the malaria drug quinine from coal tar.
choices.B: Perkin named his purple substance mauveine and opened a factory to produce it.
choices.C: Perkin's failed attempt to make quinine yielded mauveine, a lasting purple dye from coal tar that offered an alternative to expensive dyes from sources such as sea snails.
choices.D: Mauveine could dye silk, and it did not fade in sunlight or washing.

candidates.evidence: Before mauveine, purple dyes came from sources such as sea snails and were very expensive.
candidates.explanation: Significance comes from the contrast with expensive older dyes; choice C joins the discovery, the dye's durability and that contrast.

A.rationale: This gives background on the attempt but never says why the discovery mattered.

B.rationale: This reports what Perkin did next but does not explain the dye's significance.

D.rationale: This describes the dye's qualities but not why the discovery mattered compared with earlier dyes.

hints: Which note explains why the discovery was important?

strategy.explanation: Identify the goal, then look for the choice that includes the note giving significance.

candidates.remember: Synthesis choices must address the stated goal, not just repeat notes.
